questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require follow-up.

rationale.correct: Severe hypoxemia with bilateral infiltrates and normal heart function is ARDS; high tidal volume and plateau pressure need correcting.

perOption.r3: Large tidal volumes overstretch injured lungs; ARDS uses about 6 mL/kg of ideal body weight.
perOption.r4: Above 30 cm H2O raises the risk of lung injury and barotrauma.

perOption.b1:c: That would be a normal or mild value.
perOption.b2:a: A ratio of 100 or less is severe ARDS.
perOption.b2:d: The ratio, timing and bilateral infiltrates without heart failure meet the definition.
perOption.b3:a: Both are common indirect causes of ARDS.

questions.stem: The provider orders lung-protective ventilation at 6 mL/kg of ideal body weight. What tidal volume should the ventilator be set to? Record your answer as a whole number.

rationale.correct: Tidal volume is based on ideal body weight, not actual weight, because lung size follows height. 66 kg x 6 mL/kg = 396 mL. Using the actual weight of 98 kg would give 588 mL and overstretch the lungs.
references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: At 1100 the high-pressure alarm sounds. Review the findings. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Disconnect and ventilate with a bag-valve device on 100% oxygen
Check the tube is still at 23 cm at the lips
Silence the alarm and recheck the client in 10 minutes
Increase the PEEP setting to improve the oxygenation
Suction the airway and wait to see if the SpO2 improves

rationale.correct: A sudden high-pressure alarm with one-sided absent breath sounds, tracheal shift and hypotension is tension pneumothorax: bag on 100%, check the tube and get decompression now.

perOption.a: Removes the ventilator as a cause and supports oxygenation.
perOption.b: Absent breath sounds on one side, tracheal shift and hypotension mean tension pneumothorax.
perOption.c: Rules out displacement into a mainstem bronchus as part of the DOPE check.
perOption.d: The alarm shows a life-threatening change.
perOption.e: More pressure worsens a tension pneumothorax.
perOption.f: Suctioning does not treat tension pneumothorax.

perOption.b1:b: Needs assessment, but the client is still oxygenating.

questions.stem: The RN plans care while waiting for the surgeon. For each team member, select the tasks that fit their role.

options.text: Assess the chest tube system, dressing and lung sounds
Call the surgeon with an SBAR report
Empty the drainage unit to measure it
Mark the drainage level on the unit every hour and report it
Decide whether the air leak comes from the client or the tubing
Take vital signs every 15 minutes and report a systolic below 100
Strip the chest tube to keep it draining

rationale.correct: The RN assesses and communicates; the LPN measures marked drainage; the UAP takes vital signs against stated limits. No one empties the drainage unit or strips the tube routinely.

perOption.a: Assessment of an unstable client stays with the RN.
perOption.b: Communicating a change in condition is the RN's role.
perOption.c: A chest drainage unit is never emptied; output is marked on it.
perOption.d: A routine measurement with clear parameters.
perOption.f: Measuring and reporting is within the role.
perOption.g: Stripping is not done routinely and is not delegated.

questions.stem: At 2240, while being turned, the tubing pulls apart from the drainage unit. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Put the tube end 2 cm under sterile water
Connect a new sterile drainage system
Assess breathing, SpO2 and breath sounds
Clamp the chest tube until the surgeon arrives
Leave the chest tube open to the air for now
Reconnect the contaminated end without cleaning it

rationale.correct: A disconnected chest tube needs a temporary water seal and a new system, not prolonged clamping.

perOption.a: This makes a temporary water seal, so air cannot enter the chest.
perOption.d: Clamping for long periods with an air leak can cause tension pneumothorax.
perOption.e: Air will enter the pleural space.
perOption.f: Increases infection risk; use a new sterile system.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of opioid-induced respiratory depression.

questions.stem: For each factor, indicate whether it raises the client's risk of respiratory depression.

rows.text: Untreated obstructive sleep apnea without CPAP
A basal (continuous) PCA rate
Gabapentin
Diphenhydramine at bedtime
Oxygen at 4 L/min
A laparoscopic rather than open incision

rationale.correct: Several sedating drugs, a basal opioid infusion and untreated sleep apnea add up; oxygen hides the result.

perOption.r1:c1: Airway collapse during sleep worsens with sedatives.
perOption.r1:c2: Airway collapse during sleep worsens with sedatives.
perOption.r2:c1: Opioid is given even while the client sleeps.
perOption.r2:c2: Opioid is given even while the client sleeps.
perOption.r3:c1: Adds sedation and respiratory depression with opioids.
perOption.r3:c2: Adds sedation and respiratory depression with opioids.
perOption.r4:c1: A sedating antihistamine adds to CNS depression.
perOption.r4:c2: A sedating antihistamine adds to CNS depression.
perOption.r5:c1: It does not cause depression, but it hides it from pulse oximetry and delays detection.
perOption.r5:c2: It does not cause depression, but it hides it from pulse oximetry and delays detection.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize opioid-induced respiratory depression and its monitoring.

questions.stem: For each intervention, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated now.

rows.text: Stop the PCA and remove the demand button
Naloxone 0.04 mg IV, repeated every 2 to 3 minutes until breathing improves
Naloxone 2 mg IV push all at once
Let the client sleep, since the SpO2 is 93%
Raise the head of the bed and apply CPAP from the respiratory therapy department
Give the 0600 gabapentin dose as scheduled

rationale.correct: Stop the opioid, reverse it carefully with small doses, open the airway with CPAP, and hold other sedatives.

perOption.r2:c1: Small, titrated doses reverse depression without causing severe pain or withdrawal.
perOption.r2:c2: Small, titrated doses reverse depression without causing severe pain or withdrawal.
perOption.r3:c1: A full dose can cause sudden severe pain, hypertension, pulmonary edema and dysrhythmias in a postoperative client.
perOption.r3:c2: A full dose can cause sudden severe pain, hypertension, pulmonary edema and dysrhythmias in a postoperative client.
perOption.r4:c1: Sleep with an EtCO2 of 64 is dangerous.
perOption.r4:c2: Sleep with an EtCO2 of 64 is dangerous.
perOption.r6:c1: Hold sedating drugs until the provider reviews them.
perOption.r6:c2: Hold sedating drugs until the provider reviews them.

questions.educationalObjective: Generate solutions for opioid-induced respiratory depression.

exhibits.title: Standing protocol
exhibits.body: For Pasero sedation 4 or respirations below 8/min: stop opioids, give naloxone 0.04 mg IV every 2 minutes as needed, call the rapid response team.

questions.stem: After two doses of naloxone, the client's respirations are 14/min. Which actions should the nurse take next? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor sedation and EtCO2 closely for the next 2 hours
Tell the provider and ask for a non-opioid pain plan
Keep the client on CPAP while asleep
Restart the PCA at the same settings once awake
Stop monitoring once the client is talking
Give diphenhydramine to help the client go back to sleep

rationale.correct: Naloxone is short-acting: watch for recurrence, change the pain plan and treat the sleep apnea.

perOption.a: Naloxone wears off in 30 to 90 minutes, before morphine does, so depression can return.
perOption.b: Pain will return once the opioid is reversed.
perOption.c: Treats the sleep apnea that added to the risk.
perOption.d: The same settings caused the event.
perOption.f: Another sedative would add to the risk.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of tracheostomy obstruction.

questions.stem: For each finding, choose the most likely cause.

cells.text: A suction catheter passes, but returns a thick plug of mucus and air movement improves
The suction catheter cannot pass, the client can speak, and the tube sits further out than marked
Air and sound escape from the mouth during ventilation

options.text: Mucus plug in the tube or airway

rationale.correct: A passable catheter with a plug means obstruction; a catheter that will not pass with a tube further out means dislodgement.

perOption.b1:b: A catheter usually cannot pass into the trachea.
perOption.b1:c: A leak causes air escaping from the mouth.
perOption.b2:a: A displaced tube lies outside the trachea.
perOption.b2:b: A plug would not let the client speak around a cuffed tube.
perOption.b3:d: Possible, but a leak is more likely.

questions.stem: The nurse prepares to suction the tracheostomy. For each step, indicate whether it is correct practice.

rows.text: Give 100% oxygen for 30 to 60 seconds before suctioning
Apply suction only while withdrawing the catheter
Limit each pass to 10 seconds
Use suction pressure of 80 to 120 mm Hg
Instill saline before every pass to loosen secretions
Make as many passes as needed without a break

caseStudies.title: Opioid-induced respiratory depression in sleep apnea

exhibits.title: Surgical unit, 0300
exhibits.body: A 48-year-old client with a BMI of 44 and obstructive sleep apnea had a laparoscopic hernia repair yesterday. The client's CPAP machine was left at home. Pain plan: morphine PCA 1 mg demand with a 1 mg/hour basal rate, gabapentin 300 mg three times daily, and diphenhydramine 50 mg at 2200 for sleep. Oxygen 4 L/min by nasal cannula. At 0300 the client is snoring loudly with pauses of 20 seconds and is hard to wake.

exhibits.title: Medical unit, day 10 after tracheostomy
exhibits.body: A 70-year-old client had a cuffed tracheostomy placed 10 days ago after prolonged ventilation; the stoma is now well formed. The client has a spare tracheostomy tube of the same size and one size smaller, an obturator and suction at the bedside. Humidified oxygen at 35% by trach collar.

rows.label: Breath sounds
cells: Very faint; high-pitched sound at the tube

testSets.title: NCLEX-RN adaptive exam
testSets.description: Works like the real NCLEX-RN: each question depends on your answers so far, and the exam stops once your result is clear, after 85 to 150 questions. Choose timed (5 hours) or untimed. No going back; answers and rationales at the end. The questions are being rewritten to real NCLEX difficulty and recalibrated, so treat your result as a practice estimate.
